To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
The frequency with which the behavior of others is observed is a major factor affecting the effectiveness of cooperation and competition as contingencies of reinforcement.

(a) when both participants receive the same amount of reinforcement, cooperation is more effective than competition; (b) when participants do not receive equal amounts of reinforcement, cooperation and competition are equally effective, but the former is more effective when the ratio of reinforcers is 1:1 and the latter is more effective when it is 2:1; and (c) the effects of the contingencies are not affected by the number of participants.

the number of responses emitted by participants in cooperative and competitive dyads is a joint function of the number of responses of the partner and the ratio of the number of opportunities for each participant to audit the other's performance.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of the interdependence of reinforcement contingencies on the social behavior of individuals.

the following: (1) the effects of the number of participants on behavior maintained by a particular contingency, (2) the effects of information about reinforcement and performance on the behavior of individuals in cooperative and competitive contingencies, (3) the effects of social versus nonsocial reinforcer delivery and performance information on cooperative and competitive behavior, and (4) the effects of different reinforcement contingencies on cooperative and competitive performance and the behavior of participants in cooperative and competitive situations.
the effects of the social environment on behavior and the effects of behavior on the social environment.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
cooperation is more effective than competition in producing high levels of behavior, but that this is not necessarily true when cost-effectiveness is a consideration.
the experimental analysis has not yet addressed the issues of interest in social psychology and behavior analysis with regard to interpersonal relations.
cooperation and competition are not equivalent.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the social relations literature has been a fertile area for the application of behavioral concepts and methods, and the experimental analysis of social relations provides a perspective and a method for further investigation of this literature.
the effects of social contingencies depend on the nature of the contingency, the nature of the response, and the history of the participants.
cooperation and competition are not necessarily mutually exclusive, and that the relative effectiveness of the two contingencies is not a simple function of the number of participants.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the experimental analysis of social behavior has a lot to offer the study of social behavior in general and interpersonal relations in particular.

the experimental analysis of human behavior can be used to investigate social behavior in a manner that provides a better understanding of the controlling variables than is available from other approaches.
we should not be too quick to dismiss the importance of social relations for the control of behavior.
